Howard Lutnick's sons' Nvidia ties amid Jensen Huang China spy scandal
Cantor Fitzgerald’s reported Nvidia share count fell by nearly half between September 2025 and March 2026, a CNBC analysis found.
That was the period when, according to Axios, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick faced pressure from administration officials to address suspected smuggling of Nvidia's advanced AI chips to China.
The Wall Street firm, which Lutnick formerly chaired and is now run by his sons, maintained extensive commercial ties to Nvidia, helping arrange billions of dollars in financing for companies in its AI business universe and repeatedly hosting its top executives.
Those relationships have come into sharper focus following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s resignation and revelations about Lutnick’s handling of national security concerns involving the chipmaker. There is no evidence that Cantor's business interests influenced Lutnick's decisions.
Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick looks on as President Donald Trump speaks in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, D.C., U.S., June 11, 2026.
In late September, Cantor Fitzgerald hosted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and other top executives from the chipmaker for investor meetings in New York, according to a Cantor research report reviewed by CNBC.
"We continue to view NVDA as the best risk/reward in our coverage," Cantor analyst C.J. Muse and his colleagues wrote in a research report dated Oct. 3 that maintained a $350 price target and overweight rating on the stock.
Yet the firm, formerly run by Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and now led by his sons, Brandon and Kyle, reported a nearly 50% decline in the number of Nvidia shares it held between September 2025 and March 2026 , according to a CNBC analysis of securities filings that excludes options. Nvidia had been one of the largest stock positions reported in Cantor's filings.
The decline coincided with White House and U.S. intelligence officials pressing Lutnick to crack down on Megaspeed , a Singapore-based company suspected of funneling Nvidia's advanced artificial intelligence chips to China . Lutnick repeatedly resisted those efforts, Axios reported Nov. 11.
By the time Cantor hosted Huang in New York, Lutnick had also received a classified intelligence warning, according to a Nov. 10 Axios report, about Huang's ties to a suspected Chinese spy and had appeared alongside the CEO at a G20 technology summit in North Carolina.
Even as Cantor pared back its Nvidia stake, it continued doing business across the chipmaker's AI empire. A CNBC review of securities filings, corporate announcements and Wall Street research found the firm has helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for Nvidia's business partners while maintaining close ties to the chipmaker's leadership.
Those ties have drawn fresh scrutiny following Huang's resignation Thursday and Axios' reporting that Lutnick repeatedly resisted a crackdown on companies suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips to China, despite President Donald Trump authorizing new export restrictions on those companies for a third time on Nov. 5.
An ethics expert said the relationship between Lutnick and his former firm's investments may raise questions, given what the secretary knew about Nvidia.
Richard Painter , the former chief White House ethics lawyer for President George W. Bush and now a corporate law professor at the University of Minnesota, said that while "there's no proof of" Lutnick sharing nonpublic information with Cantor Fitzgerald, "the appearance doesn't look great."
"His conversations with his sons better be about publicly available information," Painter told CNBC.
There is no evidence that Lutnick's sons had advance knowledge of the intelligence concerns, that changes in Cantor's reported holdings were tied to any warnings or that the firm's business interests influenced their father's decisions.
"Cantor has to date from time to time had only immaterial stand-alone proprietary positions in Nvidia, unlike the positions reflected in 13F filings which were entered into in the ordinary course of business in connection with client swap transactions, that are common in institutional markets," a Cantor spokesperson told CNBC.
Cantor declined to answer CNBC's other questions. The Commerce Department, the White House, Howard Lutnick, Brandon Lutnick and Kyle Lutnick did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment or detailed questions about the findings.
As scrutiny of Huang intensified, Cantor Chairman Brandon Lutnick was publicly praising the chipmaker's leadership. "Nvidia is one of the great companies on the planet, and they have an amazing leadership team," Brandon Lutnick told Fox Business on Wednesday.
Trump is standing by Howard Lutnick. A White House official told Reuters on Thursday that the president maintains "complete confidence" in the commerce secretary.
But cracks in the administration's unity emerged Friday, when Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that the departments of Treasury, Defense and State and the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative all "were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months."
Bessent pointed to Commerce as the department responsible for imposing the entity list, which identifies restricted businesses and other groups, adding, "You will have to ask them about their internal processes."
CEO of Nvidia Jensen Huang (L) and U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick listen during an announcement to renovate Washington Dulles International Airport, in the Oval Office of the White House on July 29, 2026 in Washington, D.C.
Nvidia was Cantor's second-largest reported stock position before Howard Lutnick left Wall Street to become commerce secretary in February 2025, behind only bitcoin investor MicroStrategy, now known as Strategy . At the end of 2024, the firm disclosed more than 3.5 million Nvidia shares worth $479 million, according to its quarterly securities filing .
That share count held steady through September 2025, but its value climbed 36% to $652 million, according to Cantor's quarterly securities filing , as the Trump administration moved over the summer to ease restrictions on Nvidia's H20 chip sales to China .
Over the following six months, however, the number of Nvidia shares Cantor reported holding fell by 49%, to 3 million in December and 1.78 million by the end of March 2026 , with their value dropping from $652 million to $310 million, according to a CNBC analysis of securities filings.
Pressure on Howard Lutnick was also mounting on Capitol Hill. Sens. Jim Banks, R-Ind., and Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., in March urged the secretary to suspend or reconsider Nvidia's export licenses after three people linked to Nvidia customer Super Micro Computer were indicted on charges of conspiring to smuggle AI chips to China.
"The Trump administration, I think, leaks like a sieve when it comes to nonpublic government information getting to various hedge fund guys," Painter said, though he stressed there is no evidence Howard Lutnick had shared such information with his sons.
The filings do not establish why Cantor's reported share count fell or whether its overall financial exposure to Nvidia declined. Nvidia’s stock had more than doubled from its April 2025 lows by late October, before retreating in the following months. The stock fell about 6.5% between the end of September and the end of March.
Cantor's reported Nvidia holdings remained near that lower level through June 30 , the latest quarter covered by public disclosures, at 1.81 million shares. Its next quarterly filing is due Monday.
Most of those shares were attributed to CF Secured , a Cantor brokerage subsidiary that uses stocks and derivatives to hedge customer transactions, according to its audited financial statements. Cantor also disclosed substantial Nvidia options positions during the time period CNBC examined, overwhelmingly skewed toward put options, which can protect against declines in the stock price.
As concerns about Huang escalated inside the Trump administration in May, according to the Nov. 11 Axios report, Cantor was helping finance the expansion of one of Nvidia's newest business partners, securities filings show .
On May 7, Nvidia and Australia-based cloud computing provider IREN announced a five-year, $3.4 billion cloud computing contract and a strategic partnership giving the chipmaker the right to invest up to $2.1 billion in IREN.
"That's not a passive financial investment. Nvidia is a partner who wins as we deliver," IREN co-CEO Daniel Roberts told investors on the company's quarterly earnings call that day.
Five days later, as Trump headed to China aboard Air Force One, Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned him about Huang's relationship with a suspected Chinese spy, The New York Times reported Tuesday. Huang, who had not initially been invited on the trip, joined the president's delegation during a refueling stop in Alaska.
Howard Lutnick had already been sent a highly classified intelligence memo detailing concerns about Huang's relationship, according to the Nov. 10 Axios report.
On May 12, the day Trump departed for China, IREN announced the pricing of a convertible bond offering that ultimately raised $3 billion when it closed two days later. Cantor was one of seven bookrunners on the deal, alongside JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs .
On the day the offering closed, May 14, Lutnick's Commerce Department quietly cleared roughly 10 Chinese companies , including Alibaba and ByteDance, to buy Nvidia's advanced H200 chips, though some of those approvals predated the intelligence memo.
It is unclear when IREN hired Cantor for the offering or how much the firm earned from the deal. Cantor declined to answer CNBC's questions about its work with IREN.
Cantor reported a substantial position in IREN's stock.
By the end of June, Cantor reported $115 million in IREN shares and $362 million in Nvidia shares. Together, the two companies accounted for more than 9% of the value of Cantor's reported $5.2 billion in securities holdings, excluding options, according to CNBC's analysis of the filing.
Brandon Lutnick, chairman of Cantor Fitzgerald, speaks during the Bitcoin 2025 conference in Las Vegas, Nevada, on May 29, 2025.
IREN was not the only company in Nvidia's orbit that turned to Cantor for financing.
In October 2025, Cantor advised AI infrastructure developer Lancium on a $600 million financing deal to support its data center campus in Abilene, Texas, the first site of Stargate, the massive AI infrastructure project backed by OpenAI , SoftBank and Oracle .
Newmark, a commercial real estate firm controlled by Cantor , also helped finance the Abilene campus, arranging a $7.1 billion construction loan in May 2025.
Ten months later, Nvidia agreed to invest $2 billion for a roughly 20% stake in Lancium, with up to $1 billion more tied to future milestones, The Information reported in August. Lancium , which is also backed by Blackstone, confirmed an investment and a technology partnership on Aug. 24 without disclosing financial terms.
It's unclear whether Cantor continued advising Lancium after the financing deal or played a role in Nvidia's investment. Neither Cantor nor Lancium responded to questions about the investment.
Cantor's reported ties also extend to Nvidia's supply chain.
In May 2025, days after Howard Lutnick announced the transfer of his ownership stake in Cantor to his children via trusts, Semafor reported that bankers at the firm had informally advised executives at Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. , which makes Nvidia's most advanced chips, on navigating Washington. Cantor called Semafor's report "baseless and false."
TSMC received billions of dollars in federal subsidies created during the Biden administration and administered by the Commerce Department to fund its U.S. manufacturing expansion.
Democratic senators called for an ethics investigation in December into whether the Lutnick family stood to benefit from Howard Lutnick's push to expand AI data centers.
And on Wednesday, Sens. Warren and Chris Coons , D-Del., demanded that Howard Lutnick, Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller preserve records on Nvidia's chip exports to China and intelligence warnings about Huang.
The senators questioned whether "prudent defensive counter-intelligence action was taken or national security recommendations were overruled."
"The place where I think the Trump administration has most failed here is in being persuaded by Jensen Huang and others to license the export of some advanced chips," Coons said Friday on CNBC's "Squawk Box," accusing the administration of turning a blind eye to the black market for more advanced chips.

The bond market just turned on the AI trade — and chip stocks lost more than $650 billion in two days: Chart of the Day
Wall Street just had its best week since August, and chip stocks led the way. But by Friday the rally was cracking, and the bond market had turned against the AI trade.
The PHLX Semiconductor Index ( ^SOX ) still finished the week up about 8%, with the Nasdaq 100 ( ^NDX ) up about 3.5% and the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) up about 2.5%. Most of those gains came early. From Wednesday's close through Friday, a Yahoo Finance basket of 62 chip stocks lost more than $650 billion in market value, and only three rose.
Nvidia ( NVDA ) never joined the rally. The stock fell about 13% in the week Jensen Huang resigned as CEO , its worst week since April 2025 and its sixth straight weekly loss, the longest streak since 2012. That wiped out about $570 billion in value as investors weighed Nvidia's $530 billion web of AI deals .
The damage spread to Nvidia's partners. Nebius ( NBIS ), in which Nvidia holds a stake, fell about 10% for the week after disappointing third quarter earnings . Nvidia-backed CoreWeave ( CRWV ) slid about 6% Friday, though it still finished up about 15% after strong quarterly results . Memory makers Micron ( MU ) and SK Hynix ( SKHY ), leaders of the early-week bounce, gave back roughly 3% to 4% Friday.
The charts show where the rebound ran out of steam. The chip index stalled before it got back to its 200-day moving average , a long-term trend line. The Nasdaq-100 closed back below its own similar average, and the Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) closed right at it.
The PHLX Semiconductor Index bounced off its Nov. 5 low near 9,000 but turned lower before reaching its 200-day average and the 11,100-11,200 zone that had held as a floor from May to October. · Yahoo Finance AlphaSpace Bonds stopped breaking chips' fall
During the AI sell-off, Treasurys acted as a shock absorber. The 10-year yield ( ^TNX ) fell on all six of chip stocks' down days from Oct. 22 to Nov. 6, as investors bought bonds when chips sank.
But this past week, yields rose on all three days when semis were down. The 10-year jumped about 30 basis points to about 5.15%, and the 5-year climbed about 33 basis points. For both, it was the biggest weekly rise since April 2025.
On Tuesday, Fed Governor Christopher Waller opened the door to a half-point rate hike , and hours later the October Consumer Price Index came in hot . On Friday, wholesale prices rose at their fastest annual pace in nearly four years .
Over the sell-off, every chip crash made traders doubt a hike was coming. Polymarket's odds of a Dec. 9 rate increase fell to about 66% after the Nov. 5 rout. By Friday, they were about 98%, with the odds of a half-point move up to 10%. Futures now price in about two quarter-point hikes by March 2027, up from one right after the crash.
Chips can't count on bonds to break their fall anymore.
Polymarket, Yahoo Finance There were still places to make money
The equal-weight S&P 500 ( ^SPXEW ) has beaten the regular index by nearly 8 percentage points since the Oct. 6 record, the widest gap since May 2009.
Apple ( AAPL ), Warren Buffett's Berkshire Hathaway ( BRK-B ), where he remains the chair, and Eli Lilly ( LLY ) all closed at record highs Friday.
Next up is Nvidia's earnings report Tuesday after the close, the first under interim CEO Colette Kress . Investors will want to know whether the outlook holds without Huang.
Meanwhile, the bond market isn't waiting for that report. In a note on the views of its president, Jens Nordvig, Vanda Research summed up the new backdrop: "It's a different world, but arguably one with more opportunity."

UK-EU breakthrough will allow airport-style checks at Eurotunnel to avoid border ‘chaos’
Eurotunnel owner Getlink wants to replicate ‘airport experience’ at Folkestone and Calais, without making people get out of cars
Airport-style passport and fingerprinting controls are to be introduced at Eurotunnel in an attempt to prevent “short-term and long-term chaos” in Folkestone and Calais .
In a breakthrough for travellers, the European Commission has agreed to a new system in which an “eagle eye” camera system, already used in Rome and Paris airports to supervise fingerprinting and facial imaging, will be used at the border between the UK and France.
Yann Leriche, the chief executive of Getlink, the Eurotunnel owner, said it had tried to replicate the “airport experience” but wanted to go much further.
Instead of getting out of the car and getting biometrics taken at a terminal building, holidaymakers and business travellers will now be greeted with special drive-through terminals in Folkestone and Calais.
New airport style drive-in biometrics kiosks at Eurotunnel in Calais. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian Both sides are now equipped with 120 kiosks under the case of an eagle-eye camera that will be monitored by police, similar to e-gates at airports where police are not physically present at each gate.
In the coming weeks, Leriche will meet UK and French authorities presenting a 40-page proposal to allow Eurotunnel to become a “laboratory” for an “intelligent border” using emerging tech and lessons learned from the US and Singapore.
The entry and exit system (EES) requires all third-country citizens including British passport holders to submit fingerprints and facial images as they enter and exit the Schengen area, but has been delayed for years.
EES was supposed to be active across the EU by 9 September, but nine of the 27 EU member states, including France , have yet to be deploy it fully because of continued technical issues.
The new drive-in fingerprinting terminals at Eurotunnel. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian It has always been a logistical nightmare for Eurotunnel and a potential cause of miles-long tailbacks at the approach to the terminal.
Originally, Getlink had planned to use a tablet to hand to the passengers in their cars to allow them to self-fingerprint and capture a facial image. It also looked at a system involving passengers parking up and going into the terminal to get fingerprinting.
But both models would have required the physical presence of police officers for first-time fingerprinting.
Leriche said: “We told the authorities: it is going to be a mess. Many people are going to the wrong place and you can’t have police jumping from one place to the next to solve the issues. It would also means customers would have a bad experience, particularly at peak time.
“This is not something people in airports experience, but nobody approached this before, thinking we could have an airport experience at the border here. But we said: why not?”
Yann Leriche, the chief executive of Getlink. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian He said that after “many, many discussions” with the European Commission and the French authorities, finally they were “authorised” to trial “eagle-eye cameras” at each kiosk. “The French authorities are also on board because for them it is more efficient, too, so we are all aligned on the trial,” he said.
The trial will last two years, but Eurotunnel hopes the experiment will become permanent.
Each car will be able to pull up to an individual kiosk, with two stands per vehicle to read passports and take fingerprints and facial images. “It will prevent the chaos in the long term and the short term and if the experiment works, as hopefully it will, then it will become permanent,” said Leriche.
He said the company had been inspired by visits to the US/Mexico border controls, where drivers and passengers remain in their cars.
The new drive-in border controls at Eurotunnel. Photograph: Graeme Robertson/The Guardian The requirement of having a police officer present each time a first-time passenger, or “primo” as they are known, submits their fingerprints was designed as a safeguard against subterfuge. Criminals, for example, could use a fellow passenger for example with a “clean skin” fingerprint.
Leriche said he had no idea when the system will be introduced by France. “It has been delayed and delayed and delayed, but our kiosks are there, they can function but the connection with the French system is still not working. It is a question we are asking all the time.”
This week it emerged that the EU had filed a lawsuit against IBM and two other companies involved in the implementation of EES.

For more than a decade, Fatih Birol has been one of the world’s most influential voices in energy markets. As the head of the International Energy Agency (IEA), he advises presidents and energy ministers; CEOs follow his view of the market with careful attention.
When we caught up at the United Nations climate change conference, known as COP31 , currently underway in Antalya, Turkey, he offered a blunt analysis: the war in Iran has unleashed a structural shift. "I don't see any credible pathway in which the world of energy is going back where it was before the Iran War," he said on Nov. 13.
A quick analysis might boil this shift down to simple terms. In general, the focus on energy security will mean more renewable energy because it can be produced locally. It will mean efficiency measures so that countries use less fuel and are less vulnerable to shocks. Indeed, an energy crisis policy tracker from the IEA cites dozens of policies countries have laid out this year to do just that—from a push for biodiesel in Indonesia to incentives for consumers to install solar and storage in Bangladesh.
By signing up you are agreeing to our Terms of Service and Privacy Policy .
But Birol says the coming structural changes in energy will have even wider implications, shaping economic and geopolitical outcomes. He cites economic diversification plans from oil-exporting countries, new trade partnerships, and investments in new technologies like next-generation batteries and nuclear power. All of which comes with an eye toward safeguarding energy supply from supply disruptions. "Instead of importing energy, they are deciding to build energy,” he told me.
A key theme in Antalya—and on Birol’s mind—is electrification. Right now less than a quarter of final energy consumption comes from electricity. The rest comes primarily from fuel consumption, think of petrol in vehicles, heating oil in homes, or gas in stoves. Relying on electricity, which tends to be produced relatively close to where it’s used, addresses energy security concerns. That’s even more the case when electricity is produced using renewables rather than imported fossil fuels.
The COP31 presidency is pushing countries to pledge to rely on electricity for 35% of their final energy consumption by 2035. The world’s electricity grid still relies on fossil fuels to some degree—more or less so depending on the area—but today it’s typically cleaner than most fossil fuels. It will be even cleaner as renewable deployment continues.
Electrification also represents a structural shift. It promises to reshape trade relationships as countries need to either build clean technology supply chains or identify friendly partners to build relevant trade relationships. It will spur investment in the power sector, advancing both big electric infrastructure projects and creating new companies that build innovative electricity technologies. In the IEA’s special report on electrification released in September, the agency says that annual global investment in electricity generation, battery storage, and grids could total $2.5 trillion by 2035 in a scenario where electrification really takes off. That’s a $1 trillion increase from last year. And electrification promises to unlock—or at least lessen—the stranglehold that oil and gas has on geopolitics while elevating the importance of another set of resources, including critical minerals.
“Two years ago, I said we are entering the age of electricity,” Birol told me. “I can tell you today, when I look at today's numbers, we are in the age of electricity."

Ukrainian soldiers run toward their positions through a ‘kill zone’ exposed to Russian drone attacks in the Druzhkivka area of eastern Ukraine’s Donetsk region. Photograph: Kostiantyn Liberov/Libkos/Getty Images
Ukrainian soldiers run toward their positions through a ‘kill zone’ exposed to Russian drone attacks in the Druzhkivka area of eastern Ukraine’s Donetsk region. Photograph: Kostiantyn Liberov/Libkos/Getty Images
Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy says Starshield restrictions continue on ‘entire front line’
Curbs on SpaceX system are making it hard to intercept drones and sending a bad signal to Russia, says Ukrainian president. What we know on day 1,725
Volodymyr Zelenskyy has said ⁠speed restrictions remain in place on the US Starshield satellite communications system , hampering ⁠the Ukrainian military’s ability ⁠to ​operate inside the country. The continued restrictions made it hard to intercept jet-powered and other ⁠drones and sent a bad signal to Russia on dealing with land seized by Russian forces ⁠in the war, the Ukrainian president also said on Friday. “Unfortunately, the speed restrictions remain in place ​along the entire front line ‌and in temporarily-occupied ‌territories of Ukraine,” he said in his nightly video address. “I expect ‌the ministry of defence and the foreign ministry, together with all relevant structures in the United States, will work through this issue.” Ukrainian officials said in mid-October that Elon Musk’s SpaceX had abruptly capped the speed of Starlink and its Starshield military version amid tensions with ​the US over Ukrainian attacks on Russian oil refineries. Service was restored on 24 October.
Zelenskyy said on Thursday Ukrainian military units had recorded ​disruptions to ​Starshield over several days. He repeated that the restrictions “limit our ​ability to ‌intercept jet-powered ​Shaheds [Iranian-designed drones] ​and counter other drones”. “They also send Russia a signal that America may somehow treat our temporarily-occupied land differently,” he said. “We expect the speed to be restored.”
Russia attacked a hospital in the centre of Kyiv, close to several western embassies , after Zelenskyy’s comments on the throttling of Starshield . Three people were injured when a drone smashed into the National Institute of Traumatology and Orthopedics at 3am, hitting the second floor of the hospital and an adjoining 19th-century building in the capital, reports Luke Harding . Meanwhile, Russia claimed to have shot down nearly 1,200 Ukrainian drones overnight, one of the largest swarms sent by Kyiv. It said at least four people were killed in the southern region of Volgograd.
The EU’s foreign policy chief warned against “walking into the traps that Russia is setting” as she said Moscow was trying to start a debate about European security in order to divert attention from its aggression, reports Jennifer Rankin . “We have one aggressor and one victim, and the aggressor does not have security concerns,” Kaja Kallas said on arrival at an EU leaders’ summit in Dublin. In talks on the Ukraine war, Russia has revived its hardline demands for a total overhaul of European security – demands that were rejected in 2021.
Russia has been rocked by two car bomb attacks that killed a senior military figure and seriously injured a suspected intelligence agent, in the latest in a series of assassination attempts believed to have been orchestrated by Kyiv. On Friday morning a car bomb exploded in southern Moscow, severely injuring Sergei Zavorotniy, 72, a former senior aide to Ukraine’s exiled former prime minister Mykola Azarov, reports Pjotr Sauer . The blast came a day after a car bomb explosion in St Petersburg killed a senior Russian military official. items.title: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent points finger at Howard Lutnick, Commerce Department over Nvidia chip scandal - New York Post
items.summary: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent points finger at Howard Lutnick, Commerce Department over Nvidia chip scandal  New York Post
items.content:
WASHINGTON — Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blamed the Commerce Department — and by extension, his cabinet colleague Howard Lutnick — for the Trump administration not acting sooner against a Nvidia customer accused of illegally diverting sensitive AI chips to China.
It’s the highest-profile, most public criticism to date to fall upon Lutnick, who is facing accusations that his agency failed to properly investigate Megaspeed for sending advanced AI chips to China, which was against US trade rules.
The embattled Commerce secretary is set to testify before the Senate in early December about his agency’s handling of AI chip export controls.
Chinese President Xi Jinping greets US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent with Jensen Huang (center) in Beijing, May 14, 2026. REUTERS
Critics on Capitol Hill are questioning why the agency didn’t blacklist Megaspeed – a Singapore-based firm led by Alice Huang, the alleged Chinese spy who had an affair with Jensen Huang, no relation. Commerce did not take action even as US officials grew concerned Megaspeed was smuggling advanced chips to China.
The revelation of Jensen Huang’s affair with Alice Huang and concerns that Commerce slow-walked restrictions on Megaspeed have created the perfect storm around Lutnick, who previously clashed with colleagues over his support for Trump’s reciprocal tariffs.
Bessent told CNBC’s “Squawk Box” Friday morning that four executive departments favored putting Singapore-based Megaspeed on a list of companies that posed national security concerns, but faced inaction by Lutnick’s agency.
“Treasury, War, [The Office of the US Trade Representative], and State were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months, but Commerce has the pen,” Bessent said. “You will have to ask them about their internal processes.”
Lutnick is not popular with fellow members of the Trump administration.
According to multiple reports, Bessent confronted Lutnick last week over the Commerce Department’s inaction on Megaspeed, with the Commerce secretary only responding that he would “look into it.”
Bessent speaks during a press conference in St. Cloud, Minn., Oct. 30, 2026. Leila Navidi/Minnesota Star Tribune via AP
“We don’t repeat conversations in the Situation Room,” Bessent told CNBC pointedly when asked about the dispute.
President Trump, however, is standing by Lutnick — for now. The two men are longtime friends from New York City, sharing a love of the Knicks and moving throughout the charity social circuit together.
“Secretary Lutnick is a champion of President Trump’s America First trade and tariff policies, which have secured almost 20 fair trade deals and trillions in manufacturing investments,” a White House official told The Post Friday.
“President Trump maintains complete confidence in the secretary and his ability to carry out the position as the most transformative Commerce secretary in modern history.”
Jensen Huang described Lutnick as his closest friend in the administration and spoke to him often.
When President Trump nominated Lutnick to lead the Commerce Department, his Cantor Fitzgerald firm held about $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock.
The firm is now run by Lutnick’s sons, Brandon and Kyle. Its Nvidia share count fell by nearly half between September 2025 and March 2026, a CNBC analysis found.
That was the same time period the Commerce secretary faced pressure from administration officials to address suspected smuggling of Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China via Megaspeed.
Rumblings about “bad findings about Megaspeed” had swirled within the agency as far back as the summer of 2025, a recently departed Commerce official told The Post.
President Donald Trump greets Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick at a campaign rally in Greenville, N.C., Tuesday, Oct. 20, 2026. AP Photo/Matt Ramey
At the same time, Jensen Huang was lobbying administration officials to open up sales of Nvidia’s chips, including to China.
A former Commerce Department official told The Post that the agency was close to publishing a rule in July 2025 requiring export licenses for advanced chip sales to certain countries in Southeast Asia and received sign-off from other relevant agencies – but Lutnick “refused to publish it.”
The investigation into whether or not Megaspeed sent chips to China was removed from Commerce late last year and turned over to the Justice Department after Nvidia’s general counsel contacted investigators at the former department to ask for an update.
Bessent also said Nvidia staff should be investigated about what they knew about Megaspeed.
“Did Nvidia know their client?” the Treasury secretary asked rhetorically. “Was there a robust effort at Nvidia to make sure that there was no leakage and that they weren’t selling to what were obviously pass-through shell companies [for China]? I think it’s important that anyone at the company there be held accountable for that.”

History says the short term could be shaky, but the market's long-term future is bright.
There's been no shortage of market volatility over the last week. After experiencing their worst week of 2026 in early November, the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC -0.40% ) , Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC -0.91% ) , and Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI +0.10% ) are rallying once again.
However, that doesn't mean that investors are in the clear. The tech industry is still struggling with volatility -- especially after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's recent ousting -- and the market is the priciest it's been in decades.
Warren Buffett has also issued a direct warning to investors who may be underestimating market risk right now, and history has both good and bad news about what's coming next.
During Berkshire Hathaway 's 2026 meeting, Buffett discussed his thoughts on the current market in an interview with CNBC. He warned that in this historically expensive market, some investors are taking on too much risk.
"I've compared the markets to a church with a casino attached," he noted, with the church representing fundamentals-based long-term investing and the casino depicting short-term buying.
[T]he casino has gotten very attractive to people," Buffett warned, adding, "that's not investing, it's not speculating, it's gambling." He emphasized, however, that "that doesn't mean that investing is terrible. It does mean that prices for an awful lot of things will look very silly."
The S&P 500 has notched more than two dozen record highs so far in 2026, but the downside to all of that growth is that some stocks are at risk of becoming overvalued.
The S&P 500 Shiller CAPE Ratio measures the S&P 500's valuation over time based on its 10-year inflation-adjusted earnings. The higher the metric climbs, the more likely the index is overvalued and due for a pullback.
While no market indicator can predict when recessions or bear markets will begin, this particular metric has a long track record of preceding downturns. In 1929, for example, it spiked just before the Great Depression began. It surged again in 1999, during the dot-com bubble. Most recently, it peaked in late 2021, just months before stocks sank into a bear market.
In 2026, this metric reached its highest level since the dot-com bubble burst -- surpassing 40 for only the second time in stock market history. While this doesn't necessarily mean a crash is imminent, it does mean the market is incredibly richly valued right now.
The market may be pricey, but that doesn't mean it's a bad time to buy. It's crucial, however, to maintain a long-term outlook.
As Buffett mentioned, not all investing is bad. While some stocks may be overvalued right now, there are still plenty of fairly priced and even undervalued stocks with plenty of room for growth.
History also proves time and again that quality stocks will thrive over time. Since 2000, for example, the S&P 500 has faced the dot-com bubble, the Great Recession, the COVID-19 crash, the 2022 bear market, and countless smaller corrections along the way. It's also up by nearly 750% in that time.
It's impossible to say where the market is headed in the near term. But if history has just one lesson for investors, it's that healthy stocks and a long-term outlook are the keys to surviving whatever volatility may be looming.

items.title: Jojo the gorilla has spent his life alone. Can he finally find a companion?
items.summary: Jojo was poached as an infant and grew up in captivity. His keepers want to find him a friend - but it's not straightforward.
items.content:
In 2015, a young male gorilla named Jojo took his first tentative steps onto grass.
Until that moment, the 11-year-old ape had spent almost his entire life in a tiny cage at a private zoo in Gabon, after being taken from the wild as an infant. His family had been killed by the poachers who took him.
More than a decade later, Jojo is settled into a sanctuary â but he still lives alone. He hasn't had a family since he was taken, or indeed any gorilla friends.
Jojo's carers at the Lekedi Foundation in Gabon want to find a companion - possibly another rescued or zoo-bred gorilla â that Jojo could live and bond with. But finding him a friend - and bringing them into his life - is not straightforward.
"He's probably the most extreme case of isolation I've ever seen in a great ape," says Prof Gillian Forrester from the University of Sussex, who is studying Jojo as part of research into great ape psychology and how to help rescued animals recover from trauma.
Figure caption, Jojo's keeper Maxe Anaclet Makaba: 'He definitely feels lonely - you can see it in his eyes'
Jojo was less than a year old â an infant clinging to his mother â when he was captured and sold.
Most gorillas spend the first 14 to 19 years of their life in an embedded family unit but he was kept completely alone and on public display at the private zoo that bought him.
Maxe Anaclet Makaba, who is head keeper at Lekedi and sees Jojo nearly every day, says it is clear he "craves human interaction".
"He will even go to the trouble of gathering leaves for us to hold, so that we [trade them] for a treat â to interact with us," he says.
Jojo also calls out when women he knows well visit his enclosure and then leave, making sounds that silverback males use to summon the females in the wild, explains Ãric Willaume, who runs the sanctuary.
Image caption, When Jojo first arrived at the sanctuary after spending years in a small iron cage, he didn't look directly at people
Jojo is one of the more than 6,000 African primates estimated to have been bought or sold in the global trade of apes and other primates between 2000 and 2023. Thousands more are trafficked illegally for use as exotic pets, wild meat, and traditional medicine, the Pan African Sanctuary Alliance says. , external
Experts believe when baby great apes are taken from their group at a young age like Jojo, they are left traumatised.
"If they're old enough to understand what happened to them, to understand their family was killed, they just lose the will to live," explains conservationist Tony King, from UK charity the Aspinall Foundation. "You see it in their eyes â the light goes out. I never knew where that expression came from, but I've seen it in gorillas."
King â who specialises in rehabilitating rescued great apes â remembers rescuing two infant sister gorillas who were brought to a sanctuary in the Congo Basin.
"They were clinging to each other," he says. "They stayed together in a little tight ball for about three days before they sort of unravelled. I think that's what kept them alive."
Image caption, Sisters Likendze and Matoko clutch each other after they were brought in a wooden crate to the Project Protection des Gorilles sanctuary in the Congo
African charity the Gorilla Rehabilitation and Conservation Education (Grace) Center uses what it calls "gorilla-led" rehabilitation. When the team rescues a young gorilla from the pet trade, they put it with a group as soon as possible so they can socialise and essentially learn to be a gorilla.
But Jojo's case is unusual. He is fully mature and showing signs of harmful, chronic stress, according to Forrester.
In a game-changing approach to studying anxiety and trauma in apes, she has used a thermal camera to film Jojo's face. This allows her to monitor blood flow, revealing what appears to be a chronically cold nose.
It's a sign of a malfunctioning stress response. When any primate â a human, chimp or gorilla - is stressed, blood flow to the eyes and ears increases. It puts them on high alert for danger, but leaves their nose, temporarily, colder. For Jojo, this "nasal dip" as it is known, does not seem to recover.
"Being connected to others is incredibly important to our psychology as great apes," Forrester says. "Having another individual to share his life with would be so healing for him.
"I would assume other gorillas would help him process this grief and trauma."
Image caption, Thermal imaging of Jojo's face reveals signs of chronic stress, with a persistently cold nose indicating a potentially disrupted stress response
Dr Katie Fawcett, from the Grace Center, says it's also "essential" for an animal to form social relationships to be considered for release into the wild - which is the ultimate goal for Jojo's keepers.
The bonds between gorillas â what we would call friendship - is key to their society, adds Dr Robin Morrison from the University of Zurich, who studies the social lives of mountain gorillas. In one recent study, she discovered that female mountain gorillas would seek out females they knew, even if they hadn't seen them for many years, when joining a group.
And she says a big part of a gorilla's normal social life is "just sitting together quietly sharing space".
But Jojo has never been given the opportunity to sit quietly with another gorilla.
No one knows how Jojo will react to a companion. Moving an animal from an accredited zoo would be a decision for an international committee and based on genetics, health and the animals' personalities and compatibility.
Any introduction to another animal would be done very carefully â perhaps giving them an object that smells of the other before they see each other.
These slow, cautious ape introductions do happen â when an animal moves from one zoo group to another, for example. Forrester has contacted a number of accredited zoos to explore the possibility of doing this for Jojo. But those discussions have fizzled out with no sign of progress.
The problem, she says, is "there aren't clear processes in place to do these kinds of trans-locations".
Image caption, Encounters between two or more separate gorilla groups are complex social events
The international rules and processes for moving captive gorillas across international borders - from one zoo or safari park to another - are designed for breeding programmes.
"They're not designed for reintroductions into the wild, or to find companions for animals that might need them," says Forrester.
And because Jojo, who is probably in his 20s, has reached maturity, King thinks it might be too late for him to bond with other gorillas.
"Jojo's situation is unique, but he is probably best where he is," King says, adding that introducing him to another animal could, somewhat ironically, be a source of more stress for him.
Image caption, Prof Forrester studies Jojo as part of research to understand how our understanding of human mental health - particularly stress and trauma - can be applied to our great ape relatives
Being alone is also natural, even relatively common, for mature male gorillas. According to Morrison, about a third of adult males are solitary. "When they reach adolescence, they tend to disperse and spend a good chunk of their life on their own."
Solo males will try to persuade females to form a group with them, but some don't succeed and may feel lonely as a consequence, Morrison believes. "If we think of loneliness in an evolutionary context - this mismatch between the social interactions they want and the social interactions they're getting. I suspect feeling lonely is part of the natural, evolutionary drive to attract females."
But while those phases â of family life and adult solitude - play a role in wild gorilla society, Jojo was forced into solitary confinement as an infant.
Morrison believes Jojo is probably both traumatised and lonely.
"[In the wild] gorillas move together, find food together, sleep together," she says. "So much of their lives is just being with this group."
That is what Jojo's keepers, Forrester, and others want for Jojo. A friend. Maybe a female, or a compatible male.
"It would be good for him to have a companion," says keeper Makaba. "Because being alone is like being cut off from the world - it's like being in prison.
"Having another gorilla there would be a good thing for him."

The 18-month programme would use horizontal drilling and multi-stage hydraulic fracturing to e xtract oil and gas from formations that conventional drilling has been unable to develop commercially.
The agreement was signed by the Egyptian General Petroleum Corporation and Halliburton. It covers technical studies and preparations in areas operated by the state-owned General Petroleum Company.
Egypt’s Ministry of Petroleum and Mineral Resources announced the agreement on November 12, according to the country’s State Information Service. Petroleum Minister Karim Badawi witnessed the signing.
The announcement does not mean that all 50 wells have been approved or that drilling has started. Egypt and Halliburton have not disclosed the programme’s value, financing arrangements , proposed commencement date or expected production.
The programme would apply two methods that can improve production from difficult geological formations.
Horizontal drilling allows a well to travel sideways through a productive rock layer instead of only descending vertically. Hydraulic fracturing involves injecting fluid under pressure to create openings through which trapped oil or gas can flow.
Egypt wants to employ the techniques in existing producing areas where resources remain trapped in low-permeability formations or cannot be extracted economically using conventional wells.
The partnership builds on a recent operation at the NES-8 well in Egypt’s Western Desert. Hydraulic fracturing was used to extract gas from the Abu Rawash F formation, producing almost three million cubic feet daily.
The formation’s low permeability had previously prevented commercially viable production through conventional methods.
Egypt has also applied multi-stage hydraulic fracturing at the H-18 well in the Western Desert’s Al Abyad field. The government is seeking to increase the well’s production from three million to approximately 12 million cubic feet of gas daily.
A separate preliminary study found that wider use of hydraulic fracturing in the Western Desert could potentially add between 50,000 and 100,000 barrels to Egypt’s daily oil production. However, that estimate remains subject to technical and economic assessments and should not be treated as confirmed output.
Egyptian Petroleum Minister Karim Badawi says advanced drilling technology could unlock oil and gas formations that conventional methods cannot exploit commercially. [sis.gov]
The Halliburton agreement comes as Egypt tries to narrow a widening gap between domestic gas production and consumption.
Egypt is currently Africa’s largest gas consumer. Demand rose by approximately 11% during the first seven months of this year, driven principally by record gas use in electricity generation, according to the International Energy Agency.
Imports covered about half of Egyptian demand in July, when consumption reached a record 6.4 billion cubic metres. Approximately 70% of those imports arrived as liquefied natural gas, while the remainder came through pipelines.
The country’s domestic gas production has struggled to keep pace.
Reuters reported that Egypt budgeted approximately $10.1 billion for LNG during the 2026/27 financial year. It had already spent $5.8 billion by October 6, raising the possibility that the final bill could exceed the budget.
Higher international prices have made the situation more difficult. Egypt recently ordered a further 33% reduction in gas supplied to fertiliser producers after an earlier 20% cut as the government tried to reduce its dependence on costly LNG cargoes.
Egypt has also held discussions with Shell, BP, TotalEnergies and other international companies about multi-year supply agreements covering between 15 and 18 LNG cargoes monthly.
Those contracts could cost between $8 billion and $11 billion annually, although negotiations had not been concluded when Reuters reported them in July.
The Halliburton agreement followed discussions between Badawi and the company’s chairman and chief executive, Jeff Miller, during the Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition and Conference earlier in November.
Egyptian General Petroleum Corporation chief executive Salah Abdel Karim signed the agreement with Halliburton’s Egypt country manager, Amr Azzam. Miller participated by video conference.
Halliburton will contribute drilling technology and technical expertise, but the government has not said whether the company will ultimately drill all the wells, supply equipment or work alongside other contractors.
That distinction matters. The agreement establishes the framework for studying and preparing the proposed programme; it is not yet a fully disclosed drilling contract.
If the studies prove commercially viable and the wells proceed, the programme could help Egypt recover more oil and gas from existing fields, reduce pressure on its foreign-currency reserves and limit some of its exposure to volatile international LNG prices.
Its actual impact will depend on how many wells receive final approval, how quickly drilling begins and how much commercially recoverable production they deliver.

items.title: Trump bought Nvidia stock as he helped chipmaker with change to export rule - The Guardian
items.summary: Trump bought Nvidia stock as he helped chipmaker with change to export rule  The Guardian
items.content:
Donald Trump with Jensen Huang. The former Nvidia chief executive has been described as a close Trump ally. Photograph: Evan Vucci/Reuters
Donald Trump with Jensen Huang. The former Nvidia chief executive has been described as a close Trump ally. Photograph: Evan Vucci/Reuters
Trump bought Nvidia stock as he helped chipmaker with change to export rule
President purchased up to $5m of stock before revoking Biden-era rule that limited Nvidia’s ability to sell to China
Donald Trump bought Nvidia stock worth millions of dollars as he made decisions on America’s China policy that would benefit the chipmaker, an analysis has found .
In May 2025, Trump’s administration rescinded a Biden-era rule designed to prevent the most advanced US-made AI chips from being exported to China.
This rule aimed to strengthen the US’s own chip industry and to protect America from what was widely regarded as a national security threat: the possibility that China might develop superior AI.
In the days before he rescinded the rule, Trump’s public financial disclosures indicate that he bought between $1m (£760,000) and $5m worth of Nvidia stock – a purchase noted in an analysis by the anti-corruption group DeKleptocracy.
He also bought shares in other tech companies, including Apple, Meta and Microsoft.
Why the Nvidia scandal is far from over - The Latest
The diffusion rule would have limited Nvidia’s ability to sell to what has been one of its largest markets: China accounted for about a quarter of the company’s sales between 2010 and 2022. Nvidia’s shares rose in value just after Trump announced the rescission of the rule, and after he had bought the stock.
In December 2025 Trump said he would allow Nvidia to sell H200 chips to China, a decision that was greenlit by the Department of Commerce in January 2026. This was a controversial move. H200s were one of the company’s most advanced chips – six times better than what was available in China at the time, said experts.
The Council on Foreign Relations suggested selling H200s would “supercharge” China’s future AI factories and strengthen the US’s rival.
Trump’s public financial disclosures indicate he made at least three purchases of Nvidia shares in the days after announcing this, all of them between $250,001 and $500,000.
These trades are among Trump’s larger purchases of Nvidia stock, although he appears to have made dozens of transactions involving the chipmaker’s shares since taking office.
DeKleptocracy wrote in its analysis: “While the country debates how a possible Chinese spy may have manipulated White House policy for one AI company, it must grapple with how Trump’s corruption may have motivated him to deliver the entire AI industry’s technology to China.”
The US – and the global economy – have been grappling with revelations that Jensen Huang , Nvidia’s former chief executive, had an affair with an alleged Chinese spy, Alice Huang.
Reports have suggested this relationship allowed Alice Huang’s company, Megaspeed, to obtain billions of dollars worth of Nvidia’s chips, even as other companies struggled.
Trump was twice briefed by US intelligence officials on their conclusions that Alice Huang was a Chinese asset. He did not act on this assessment.
Jensen Huang has been described as a close Trump ally and has met the president a number of times. Nvidia made a $25m contribution to Trump’s ballroom in October 2025, with Huang saying he was “delighted to be a part of it”.

items.title: Hegseth's failed impeachment was a warning to Democrats. Where will they go from here? - NPR
items.summary: Hegseth's failed impeachment was a warning to Democrats. Where will they go from here?  NPR<a href="https://news.google.com/rss/articles/CBMipgFBVV95cUxQOURyZ0lrSVFQZHl4Z0FMa1
items.content:
After the Hegseth impeachment failure, what will Democrats focus on? Democrats have been given a huge opportunity with majorities in both the House and Senate — but the balance of priorities, timing, messaging and discipline are all going to be major tests.
Hegseth's failed impeachment was a warning to Democrats. Where will they go from here?
House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., speaks during a news conference on Nov. 4, 2025, on Capitol Hill in Washington, D.C.
Democrats are not in the majority yet , but the first post-election test of their ability to get things done was a failure.
The House was unable to advance an impeachment effort of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. Eleven Democrats were no-shows for the vote. Based on the math in this vote: If those 11 had been there and if no more Republicans showed up, the attempt would have gone forward.
Now, for those who want to see Hegseth impeached, it's fair to ask why only one Republican was in favor of it, Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who led the effort , especially after an election that saw GOP wipeouts in no small measure because of the Iran war? The GOP still controls the floor, so a Democratic speaker would have been able to leave the vote open longer for the 11 to be able to cast their votes.
House votes to effectively end the impeachment effort against Pete Hegseth
But it's also fair to ask if this would have happened under Nancy Pelosi's watch? (Ironically, she was one of the 11 who didn't vote for advancing Hegseth's impeachment because she had flown back to San Francisco for a veterans' event.) Or if this kind of effort is what people want in the first place.
First, on the Pelosi point: The former House speaker and retiring congresswoman was known for the discipline she kept in her caucus. She knew where the votes were, who was voting how and why – and, most importantly, did not move forward with efforts that didn't have the votes.
Hakeem Jeffries, the heir apparent Democratic leader , is going to have the largest majority in Congress since the early 1990s. His leadership and agenda priorities are going to be scrutinized and compared to Pelosi – and this wasn't a great start to this new era.
Second, on whether impeachments are what people want to see: it depends on which people. Certainly, the Democratic base — and some beyond that — wants accountability for the Trump administration.
Voters more broadly also said corruption was a top issue in the campaign. But walking the line between reasonable accountability and oversight versus impeachments is a potential tight rope.
Democrats will have to balance the mandate they were given to bring down prices (sound familiar?) and end the war with the accountability of the Trump administration that many in the Democratic base feverishly wants and expects.
A Reuters/Ipsos poll taken after the election, found that 8-in-10 people think Democrats' focus in the first 100 days should be on the cost of living, three-quarters said lowering health care costs, 7 in 10 said lowering gas prices, while 6 in 10 said ending the Iran war and eliminating President Trump's tariffs.
Hakeem Jeffries is poised to become the first Black speaker of the House
What about investigations and impeachment? Only 40% said investigating the Trump administration should be a priority in those early days. But 71% of Democrats do want this to be a first 100 days focus. Only 36% of independents said the same.
Almost two-thirds said they are concerned that Democrats will spend too much time on investigations, which included, by the way, half of Democrats.
When it comes specifically to pursuing impeachment of Trump, only 33% said they think it would be good for the country. On the other hand, 63% of Democrats do. Only 30% of independents said it would be good for the country.
More than half also said they think Democrats should at least make efforts to work with the Trump administration. That, however, only included 40% of Democrats.
So this is going to be tricky to navigate for Democratic leadership, but a major part of a speaker's job is messaging, particularly when that speaker's party does not control the White House.
So what will Democrats focus on when they're in charge?
People are going to be watching the new Democratic majority for what it focuses on, and even with the Hegseth effort, it was clear that many conservatives were thrilled with not only how it went but that Democrats were fueling Massie's effort.
It arguably backfired and strengthened Hegseth's position within the administration. The White House and Republicans rallied around him. Even if some Republicans on Capitol Hill might have misgivings with Hegseth for one reason or another, and they and Vice President Vance think the war in Iran was the main reason for the midterm losses, opposing Democrats is far more unifying.
Politics is often (some would say too often) a team sport, and no group is more conditioned to put the T-shirt on and run the playbook than the red team.
It certainly gave Republicans more of a chance to go on offense than talking about health care, the cost of living or the war and gas prices.
Democratic leadership is certainly aware of the line it has to walk, but Jeffries is going to have to make some decisions. Asked on PBS NewsHour this week if Democrats would be impeaching more Trump officials, he said, "We will cross that bridge when we get to it."
But a House speaker is the one who builds the legislative bridges. He or she controls the agenda.
Jeffries, of course, also noted, as he has elsewhere, that affordability is a priority.
The Democratic Party gained power across the country in the midterms. Now what?
"We're committed to driving down the high cost of living in every area," he said. "That's housing, that's health care, that's groceries, that's gas, that's caregiving – to making this country affordable again for everyone."
Democrats have been given a huge opportunity with majorities in both the House and Senate — but the balance of priorities, timing, messaging and discipline are all going to be major tests.
The stakes couldn't be higher. Arguably, what Democrats focus on will lay the foundation for views of the party's competence heading into the 2028 presidential election, and they don't want to squander the advantages they have.
The Ipsos poll showed that Democrats have big leads on which party has a better plan, policy or approach for health care (42%-23%), the cost of living (40%-25%) and the economy (37%-30%).
But they have to be careful. A lot of people are not convinced that Democrats are focused on the issues that are important to them. Only 47% in the Ipsos poll said that, including only 40% of independents.
Only 44% said they're confident that Democrats are putting the best interests of the American people above their own personal interests.
So while Democrats have the wind at their backs, the jury is still out on whether people are confident in their leadership.

items.title: How Nvidia turmoil and a Democratic Congress could reshape the AI trade, according to ETF experts
items.summary: ETF experts say Nvidia’s leadership turmoil and Democratic control of Congress could shift AI demand to the benefit of other Big Tech stocks, rival chipmakers.
items.content:
Nvidia AI trade: Huang exit, Congress reshape Big Tech stock outlook
Despite new headline risks, Big Tech may keep getting bigger, say ETF experts
The largest technology stocks linked to the artificial intelligence trade could stand to benefit the most from Nvidia's woes and a Democratic-controlled Congress pushing back on data centers, according to investing experts interviewed on CNBC's " ETF Edge " earlier this week.
"We may have been put in an environment, as much as investors have sort of been looking for areas outside of Big Tech, where net-net Big Tech ends up as the winner once again," said Roundhill Investments CEO Dave Mazza, whose firm manages the Magnificent Seven ETF ( MAGS ).
Part of his bull case: Other players in the AI trade are positioned to fill Nvidia's chip demand if investors lose trust in the company after a tumultuous week that saw its iconic founder and CEO Jensen Huang resign.
"If we get into an environment where people can't trust … Nvidia, they're going to look for other sources for these chips because they need them," Mazza said during the "ETF Edge" interview, which occurred Monday as the Nvidia scandal grew but before Huang had resigned.
Discussing recent fund flow activity for the MAGS ETF, as well as for the Roundhill Neocloud ETF ( NCLD ) — which focuses on smaller market cap, specialized cloud computing companies — Mazza said, "In a weird way, [hyperscalers] may continue to benefit from this because they have the compute available. It's going to be more valuable if the demand is there."
The Roundhill Magnificent Seven ETF ended the week in the green, albeit with a gain of less than 1%, while the Roundhill Neocloud ETF was up over 1%, though earnings from top holdings Coreweave and Nebius presented a mixed picture.
CoreWeave had its best day since April 2025 on Wednesday after its latest quarterly results, while Nebius shares sank after its Thursday report. The neocloud ETF remains deeply in the red since its August 2026 launch, down 39%, amid concerns about balance sheet strength, which could linger given Nvidia's role in financing the AI buildout. CoreWeave shares sank again on Friday, and Nvidia posted its longest losing streak since 2012 after its latest weekly losses.
Performance of the Roundhill Neocloud ETF year to date in 2026.
Nvidia's interim CEO and current chief financial officer Colette Kress will have her first opportunity to reassure the market when Nvidia reports its third-quarter earnings next Tuesday. "Our focus remains on serving our customers, partners, developers and shareholders," Kress said in a statement issued on Thursday morning when the company announced Huang's exit.
Yorkville Ives partner and senior managing director Dan Ives said on "ETF Edge" on Monday that the market will remain optimistic about other AI chip players, like AMD and Alphabet, if Nvidia faces prolonged headwinds. Ives helped create the Dan IVES Wedbush AI Revolution ETF ( IVES ) while at Wedbush Securities, where he served as the managing director and global head of technology research before departing Wedbush to form his own firm earlier this year.
AMD finished trading this week up close to 13%, with Broadcom posting similar gains.
The tech-heavy Nasdaq index posted its best week since August as Nvidia's slump reshuffled the AI trade.
Yorkville Ives lowered its price target on Nvidia to $225 from $300 on Thursday after Huang's resignation, but maintained a buy rating on the stock, which finished the week at $162.85 per share.
"Nvidia remains the clear leader in GPU chips for the AI Revolution. They are roughly 2-3 years ahead of the nearest competitor and the demand trajectory the next few years is not changing because Jensen is gone," Ives wrote in a note to investors on Thursday. "The strategic roadmap is already essentially built around the next few family of chips and physical AI with 42k employees driving it. ... Valuation at roughly 10x 28 EPS is way too cheap once Nvidia gets through this storm and emerges on the other side."
The compute that does exist could become even more indispensable against the backdrop of a potential slowdown to the data-center buildout by Congress after the Democratic Party gains of Nov. 3 swept control of Congress, Mazza said.
Ives estimates that the "blue tidal wave" in Congress could mean 10% of planned data centers won't materialize on the low end, and 15%-20% on the high end, but he added that demand still outstrips supply four to one. "The compute is just that much more valuable in the capacity today than it was a week ago. So I could argue just more and more bullish, strong, get stronger," Ives said.
"The game is going to change for Big Tech. It will slow it down. But there's no overbuild, no bubble concerns. And I view that as actually a positive thing," he added.
